platforms.title: Black Poo on Iron Tablets: Normal or a Sign of Bleeding?
platforms.meta_description: Iron tablets often darken poo, but black, sticky, foul-smelling poo can mean a stomach bleed. How to tell, and when the NHS says call 111 or 999.
platforms.body_html:
You started a course of ferrous sulfate for low iron and, a few days later, the toilet bowl gives you a fright. The NHS medicines guide is reassuring and alarming on the same page. Under side effects it lists darker than usual poo, which it calls common and usually nothing to worry about. A few lines further down it says to talk to a doctor or call 111 straight away if your poo is black, tar-like or red, or if you also feel unwell. Both statements are about dark stools, so the colour alone cannot settle it. What settles it is texture, smell and how the rest of your body is coping.

Why Iron and Blood Both Turn Poo Black

Iron that your gut does not absorb travels on through the bowel and darkens the stool. It does not change the consistency much, so iron poo usually stays formed and smells like ordinary poo. Food can do the same thing: the NHS page on bleeding from the bottom notes that poo can look very dark or black if you take iron tablets or eat a lot of dark foods such as liquorice and blueberries. Pepto-Bismol is another familiar culprit. The NHS lists black poo and a black tongue as side effects of bismuth subsalicylate, the active ingredient.

Bleeding works differently. When blood leaks from the oesophagus, stomach or the first part of the small intestine, it spends hours in contact with stomach acid, digestive enzymes and bowel bacteria before it comes out. The MSD Manual consumer edition explains that this exposure is what turns it black, and that this kind of black stool, called melaena, can continue for several days after the bleeding has stopped. Digested blood gives the stool a sticky, tar-like look and a strong, distinctive smell, which is exactly how the NHS describes the warning sign: black, sticky and very smelly.

The most common source of that bleeding is a stomach ulcer. The NHS says ulcers are usually caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or regular use of painkillers like ibuprofen, and its advice for people with ulcer symptoms is not to take anti-inflammatory painkillers without speaking to a doctor first. If you are on iron and also reach for ibuprofen or aspirin most days for back or joint pain, your black poo deserves a closer look than it would otherwise get.

Colour Misleads, Texture and How You Feel Don't

  • Formed, dark, normal smell, and you feel fine: this fits iron, bismuth or a bowl of blueberries. Keep taking the tablets as prescribed and mention it at your next review.
  • Black, sticky, tar-like or unusually foul: the NHS ulcer page lists this as a reason to call 999 or go to A&E, and the ferrous sulfate leaflet says to call 111 straight away. Being on iron does not cancel the warning.
  • Dark plus symptoms: vomiting bright red blood or something that looks like ground coffee, severe tummy pain, dizziness, a racing heart or feeling faint all point towards blood loss. Call 999, and do not drive yourself to A&E.
  • Not sure: the NHS says a GP can do a test to check whether there is blood in your poo. Tell them you are taking iron, because it changes how the stool looks.

If iron upsets your stomach, that is a separate problem with its own fixes. The NHS says ferrous sulfate works best on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before or 2 hours after eating, but if it upsets your stomach you can take it with or after food. Keep tea, coffee, eggs and dairy at least 2 hours away from the dose, and ask your GP or pharmacist to review the dose or type of iron if the side effects persist. What you should not do is stop treatment on your own because the colour worried you; low iron that goes untreated has its own consequences.

So, Is Your Black Poo From the Iron?

Most of the time, yes, as long as it is formed, smells normal and you feel well. The single check worth remembering is the one the NHS keeps returning to: black and tar-like, or black with feeling unwell, is never something to wait out. Call 111 for advice, or 999 if you are vomiting blood, have severe pain or feel faint.
